meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I want to take the calculated risk; to dream and to build, to fail and to succeed. I refuse to barter incentive for a dole. I prefer the challenges of life to the guaranteed existence; the thrill of fulfillment to the stale calm of utopia'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Sam Walton, and not Thomas Paine. Dean Alfange wrote it as "An American's Creed" — in Reader's Digest by October 1952.

answer.label: Not Sam Walton — actually Dean Alfange
answer.authorDates: 1897–1989 · New York lawyer & politician, a founder of the Liberal Party of New York
answer.sourceLine: These lines are three consecutive sentences from Dean Alfange’s short prose piece “An American’s Creed” (also called simply “My Creed”), first published in This Week Magazine and reprinted in The Reader’s Digest in October 1952. The Library of Congress’s own quotation dictionary, Respectfully Quoted ↗, prints the passage word for word under Alfange’s name with that publication history. Sam Walton did not write it: it was already in Reader’s Digest in October 1952, and the first Walmart did not open until July 1962.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: This Week Magazine — the syndicated Sunday newspaper supplement; the Library of Congress entry names the magazine but gives no issue date
The Reader’s Digest, October 1952, p. 10, and January 1954, p. 122 (condensed)

source.excerpt: I do not choose to be a common man. It is my right to be uncommon—if I can. I seek opportunity—not security. I do not wish to be a kept citizen, humbled and dulled by having the state look after me. I want to take the calculated risk; to dream and to build, to fail and to succeed. I refuse to barter incentive for a dole. I prefer the challenges of life to the guaranteed existence; the thrill of fulfillment to the stale calm of utopia.
trail: Respectfully Quoted, entry 71 ↗ — the Library of Congress’s dictionary of quotations requested from the Congressional Research Service — prints these three sentences verbatim as part of “Dean Alfange, creed,” cites Who’s Who in America, 1984–85, vol. 1, p. 42, and adds: originally published in This Week Magazine, later reprinted in The Reader’s Digest, October 1952, p. 10, and January 1954, p. 122.

The Library of Congress catalogue record ↗ confirms the reference work itself: Respectfully quoted: a dictionary of quotations requested from the Congressional Research Service, edited by Suzy Platt, Washington, 1989.

Alfange’s biography ↗ gives the same publication history — the creed first in This Week, condensed in Reader’s Digest in October 1952 and January 1954 — and records that the Freedoms Foundation at Valley Forge gave him an award for the composition in 1952.

Independently of the paper trail, the rival Paine claim collapses on inspection: the complete text of Common Sense ↗ contains not one of the creed’s key words — no “dole,” “utopia,” “uncommon,” “incentive,” “beneficence” or “handout.”
source.excerptNote: Wording follows the text printed in Respectfully Quoted (Library of Congress, 1989), which took it from Alfange’s entry in Who’s Who in America, 1984–85, vol. 1, p. 42. That same entry notes the two Reader’s Digest printings were condensed and omitted a pair of clauses, so circulating versions of the creed differ in small details.

source.rightsNote: “An American’s Creed” is a mid-twentieth-century magazine piece: first published in This Week Magazine and reprinted in The Reader’s Digest in October 1952 — well after the 1931 cut-off for United States public domain. We have not examined copyright-renewal records for the original printings, so the conservative reading applies: treat the creed as in copyright and quote only short passages with attribution.

author.name: Dean Alfange
author.heading: Who Dean Alfange actually was
author.metaLine: 1897–1989 · American lawyer and politician; a founder of New York’s Liberal Party
author.bio: Dean Alfange was born in Constantinople in 1897 to Greek parents and built a career in New York politics that crossed almost every party line — he took nominations and appointments from the Democrats, the Republicans, the American Labor Party and the Liberal Party of New York, of which he was a founding member. He is remembered today for almost none of that. What survives is a 160-odd-word statement he wrote in the early 1950s, “An American’s Creed,” which the Freedoms Foundation at Valley Forge honoured in 1952 and which has been reprinted, framed and re-credited ever since.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The creed is one of the most re-credited pieces of American prose in circulation. Two false authors dominate, and a third problem is that the text itself gets rewritten in transit.

items.why: Circulated on business and entrepreneurship sites as “The Entrepreneur’s Creed” or “The Sam Walton Oath” ↗; one widely shared page runs the full text under the heading “Founder of Walmart” ↗. The chronology alone rules it out: the creed was reprinted in The Reader’s Digest in October 1952, and the first Walmart opened in July 1962 ↗. No Walton speech, letter or book is ever cited for it.

Blogs and inspirational posts hand it to Paine, sometimes with a specific citation — one business blog attributes it to Common Sense (1776) ↗. The full text of Common Sense ↗ contains none of the creed’s distinctive vocabulary: not “dole,” not “utopia,” not “uncommon,” not “incentive,” not “beneficence,” not “handout,” not even the phrase “common man.”

items.who: Nobody — but the text has been edited
items.why: The Walton-credited copies end “All this is what it means to be an entrepreneur,” where the Library of Congress text ↗ ends “All this is what it means to be an American.” Smaller changes travel with it — “a calculated risk” for “the calculated risk,” “to fail and succeed” for “to fail and to succeed.”

misattribution.truthLine: The Library of Congress’s own dictionary of quotations, compiled from questions put to the Congressional Research Service, prints these sentences under Dean Alfange’s name ↗ and traces them to This Week Magazine, then to The Reader’s Digest of October 1952.

context.heading: Why this one travels so well
lead: Alfange wrote a piece of Cold War civic rhetoric, not a business manifesto. The creed is a first-person refusal of the welfare state — “I do not wish to be a kept citizen” — published in This Week Magazine, the Sunday supplement that rode along with dozens of American newspapers ↗ and reached millions of households a week. That distribution, plus two Reader’s Digest reprints, put the text in front of an enormous audience with the author’s name attached only in small type.

Text that spreads faster than its byline eventually loses it. By the time the creed reached entrepreneurship blogs and motivational forums, the closing line had been changed from “All this is what it means to be an American” to “… to be an entrepreneur,” and the natural thing to hang a rewritten entrepreneur’s creed on was the most famous American entrepreneur available. Alfange’s own name kept the text alive in one narrow place: it ran at the end of his entry in successive editions of Who’s Who in America, which is where the Library of Congress compilers found it.
detailsBody: The version circulated under Walton’s name is not quite the one Alfange published. One widely copied posting headed “The Sam Walton Oath” ↗ has “I want to take a calculated risk,” “to fail and succeed,” a semicolon after “dole,” “humble” for “humbled,” and ends “All this is what it means to be an entrepreneur.”

The version quoted on this page — “the calculated risk,” “to fail and to succeed,” a full stop after “dole” — matches the text the Library of Congress prints. Even that source notes the two Reader’s Digest reprints dropped a couple of clauses found in the Who’s Who rendering, so a single fixed “original” wording is not on offer.
context.pull: Change the last word to “entrepreneur” and the creed needs a new author. Walton was the nearest one to hand.

sourcesVerified.claim: Respectfully Quoted (Library of Congress, 1989), entry 71, prints "I want to take the calculated risk; to dream and to build, to fail and to succeed. I refuse to barter incentive for a dole. I prefer the challenges of life to the guaranteed existence; the thrill of fulfillment to the stale calm of utopia" as part of Dean Alfange's creed, cites Who's Who in America 1984-85 vol. 1 p. 42, and states it was originally published in This Week Magazine and later reprinted in The Reader's Digest, October 1952 p. 10 and January 1954 p. 122 (the reprints lacking two clauses).

The Library of Congress catalogue record confirms 'Respectfully quoted : a dictionary of quotations requested from the Congressional Research Service', contributors Library of Congress Congressional Research Service and Suzy Platt, published Washington: Library of Congress, 1989.

Dean Alfange (December 2, 1897 - October 24, 1989), American politician and attorney, wrote a 1950s statement titled 'An American's Creed' or 'My Creed'; it originally appeared in This Week magazine, with a condensed version in Reader's Digest in October 1952 and January 1954; the Freedoms Foundation at Valley Forge gave him an award for it in 1952.

The full text of Thomas Paine's Common Sense contains none of the creed's distinctive vocabulary - zero occurrences of 'dole', 'utopia', 'uncommon', 'common man', 'incentive', 'beneficence' or 'handout'.
This Week was a nationally syndicated Sunday magazine supplement included in American newspapers between 1935 and 1969; in the early 1950s it accompanied 37 Sunday newspapers.

Ashland University Archives catalogues an artwork, catalog number 2013-030013, in the John M. Ashbrook political collection, titled 'Artwork- I do not choose to be a common man. a creed by Dean Alfange.'
Sam Walton lived March 29, 1918 - April 5, 1992, and the first true Walmart opened on July 2, 1962, in Rogers, Arkansas.

A post headed 'The Sam Walton Oath' presents the creed as a Sam Walton-related quote, in a variant reading 'I want to take a calculated risk; to dream and to build, to fail and succeed. I refuse to barter incentive for a dole;' and ending 'All this is what it means to be an entrepreneur.'

A page titled 'Sam Walton Quotes - Entrepreneur's Creed' presents the full creed under the attribution 'Founder of Walmart / The epitome of being an entrepreneur', ending 'All this is what it means to be an entrepreneur.'
A business blog post reproduces 'I do not choose to be a common man' and attributes it to Thomas Paine's 'Common Sense' (1776), with no mention of Dean Alfange.
